message.content:
**Hydrogen – A Quick Reference Guide to Its Properties**

| Category | Property | Value / Description |
|----------|----------|---------------------|
| **Basic Atomic Data** | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Isotopes | H‑1 (protium), H‑2 (deuterium), H‑3 (tritium) |
| | Natural abundance | Protium ~99.98 %, Deuterium ~0.02 %, Tritium negligible |
| | Ionization energy | 13.598 eV (first ionization) |
| | Electron affinity | –0.754 eV (negative, meaning it does not readily accept an electron) |
| | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | Atomic radius | 53 pm (covalent) |
| | Van der Waals radius | 120 pm |
| **Physical State (STP)** | State | Gas |
| | Color | Colorless |
| | Odor | Odorless |
| | Taste | Tasteless |
| | Density | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ (at 0 °C, 1 atm) |
| | Boiling point | –252.87 °C (121 K) |
| | Melting point | –259.16 °C (14 K) |
| | Specific heat (gas) | 14.304 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Molar volume | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| **Chemical Properties** | Molecular form | H₂ (diatomic) |
| | Bond type | Single covalent bond (H–H) |
| | Bond dissociation energy | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Oxidation states | +1 (as H⁺), –1 (as hydride H⁻) |
| | Acidic behavior | Acts as a proton donor (H⁺) in aqueous solution |
| | Basic behavior | Forms hydrides (e.g., LiH, NaH) where it behaves as H⁻ |
| | Reactivity | Highly reactive with many elements; forms hydrides, oxides, and organohydrogens |
| | Combustion | 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O (exothermic, releases ~286 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| | Hydrogen bonding | H₂O, acids, and many organic molecules exhibit H‑bonding; hydrogen itself is the donor in H‑bonds |
| **Isotopic Variants** | Deuterium (²H) | 2.014 u, heavier, used in NMR, heavy water (D₂O) |
| | Tritium (³H) | 3.016 u, radioactive (β⁻ decay, half‑life ~12.32 y), used in nuclear fusion research |
| **Nuclear Properties** | Fusion potential | 2 H + 3 H → 4He + n + 17.6 MeV (key reaction in stars & fusion reactors) |
| | Radioactivity | Tritium is the only naturally occurring radioactive isotope of hydrogen |
| **Applications & Uses** | Fuel | Hydrogen fuel cells (electricity generation) |
| | Rocket propellant | Liquid hydrogen + liquid oxygen (LH₂/LOX) |
| | Chemical industry | Production of ammonia (Haber process), methanol, and various organic compounds |
| | Metallurgy | Used to reduce metal ores, remove impurities |
| | Analytical chemistry | Deuterium labeling for NMR, mass spectrometry |
| | Medicine | Deuterated drugs, imaging agents |
| | Energy storage | Hydrogen storage in metal hydrides, high‑pressure tanks, cryogenic liquefaction |
| **Safety & Handling** | Flammability | Extremely flammable; wide flammability range (4–75 % H₂ in air) |
| | Explosion risk | Can form explosive mixtures with air or oxygen |
| | Toxicity | Non‑toxic, but inhalation of high concentrations can displace oxygen (asphyxiation risk) |
| | Environmental impact | Clean combustion (water vapor); no CO₂ emissions, but production processes may emit greenhouse gases |

---

### Quick Takeaways

- **Hydrogen is the simplest element**: one proton, one electron, and usually one neutron (protium).  
- **It exists mainly as a diatomic gas (H₂)** under normal conditions.  
- **Its isotopes (deuterium, tritium)** give it unique roles in nuclear fusion, medical imaging, and isotope labeling.  
- **Chemically, it can act as both an acid (H⁺) and a base (H⁻)**, forming a wide variety of compounds.  
- **Physically, it is the lightest, most abundant element** in the universe, yet it is highly reactive and flammable.  
- **Hydrogen’s future lies in clean energy**: fuel cells, hydrogen‑powered vehicles, and fusion research.

Feel free to ask for deeper dives into any of these categories—whether you want the thermodynamic data, the quantum mechanical details, or the industrial processes that harness hydrogen!
